title: What an Organism Has to Do

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: Why can a leaf in air not saturated with water vapour not take in carbon dioxide without losing water?
cards.back: Carbon dioxide comes in and water vapour goes out through the same pores, the stomata.
cards.quote: A leaf's carbon dioxide comes in, and its water vapour goes out, through the same pores.

cards.front: In the first-approximation leaf model, what sets the price (water lost per carbon dioxide gained), and what do the pores set?
cards.back: The two concentration gaps (inside the leaf minus outside) set the price. The pores set how fast gas moves; fewer or narrower pores change the price only by changing a gap, and cannot make it zero.
cards.quote: The pores set how fast gas moves; fewer or narrower pores change the price only by changing a gap, and cannot make it zero.

cards.front: Name the five problems every multicellular organism faces, used as a checklist for every organ system.
cards.back: Energy and materials; exchange and transport, including wastes; control and relative internal stability; defense; reproduction as continuation of a lineage.
cards.quote: A multicellular organism, a body of many cells that depend on one another, faces five problems.
cards.section: Five problems, one checklist for the course

cards.front: {{c1::Diffusion}} is the net movement of molecules from higher to lower concentration.
cards.quote: Diffusion, the net movement of molecules from higher to lower concentration, can do much of this in a small organism.
cards.section: Five problems, one checklist for the course

cards.front: Diffusion can handle much of the exchange in a small organism. What carries the load in a large one, in animals and in plants?
cards.back: Transport systems: blood vessels in animals; xylem and phloem in plants.
cards.quote: In a large one, transport systems carry the load
cards.section: Five problems, one checklist for the course

cards.front: In plants, what does the xylem carry, and what does the phloem carry?
cards.back: Xylem: water and minerals up from the roots. Phloem: sugars from where they are made to where they are used.
cards.quote: the phloem, which carries sugars from where they are made to where they are used
cards.section: Five problems, one checklist for the course

cards.front: {{c1::Homeostasis}} is the maintenance of a relatively stable internal environment.
cards.back: Example: adult humans hold core temperature near 37 degrees C.
cards.quote: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a relatively stable internal environment.
cards.section: Five problems, one checklist for the course

cards.front: In Arabidopsis, closing the stomata can help defend against bacteria that enter through them. Which other two of the five problems does the same closure touch, and what does that imply about its cost?
cards.back: Control and stability (plants close pores when leaves run short of water) and exchange (the same pores admit carbon dioxide, so closing cuts carbon intake). One structure serves several problems, so a solution is paid for somewhere else.
cards.quote: in the small plant Arabidopsis, closing the stomata can be part of the defense against bacteria that enter through those pores
cards.section: Five problems, one checklist for the course

cards.front: Why is reproduction treated as a problem for the lineage rather than for every individual?
cards.back: The lineage must continue, but not every individual must breed: honeybee workers rarely reproduce while a queen is present, yet the colony keeps producing queens and males.
cards.quote: honeybee workers rarely reproduce while a queen is present, yet the colony goes on producing queens and males
cards.section: Five problems, one checklist for the course

cards.front: Water loss from a leaf through its stomata, the pores between pairs of guard cells, is called {{c1::transpiration}}.
cards.quote: the pores between pairs of guard cells; that water loss is transpiration
cards.section: Where the price comes from: one leaf, one lung

cards.front: In the leaf model, why does stomatal conductance cancel out of the water price?
cards.back: Both gases take the same path: carbon in = conductance × CO2 gap; water out = 1.6 × conductance × water vapour gap. Dividing gives price = 1.6 × water vapour gap / CO2 gap.
cards.why: Water vapour, a lighter molecule, diffuses about 1.6 times faster than carbon dioxide.
cards.quote: Divide the second line by the first and the conductance cancels
cards.section: Where the price comes from: one leaf, one lung

cards.front: In moderately dry air the water vapour gap across a leaf's stomata is about 100 times the carbon dioxide gap. About how many water molecules does the leaf lose per carbon dioxide gained?
cards.back: Price = 1.6 × water gap / CO2 gap = 1.6 × 100 = 160 water molecules per CO2; roughly 150 to 300 as the CO2 inside the leaf runs a little higher or lower.
cards.quote: so the leaf pays about 1.6 × 100 = 160 water molecules per carbon dioxide
cards.section: Where the price comes from: one leaf, one lung

cards.front: A leaf with unchanged stomata is moved from hot, dry air into humid air. What happens to its water lost per carbon dioxide gained, and why?
cards.back: It falls. Humid air shrinks the water vapour gap, and the price is 1.6 × water vapour gap / CO2 gap.
cards.quote: Humid air shrinks the water gap and the price; hot, dry air raises both.
cards.section: Where the price comes from: one leaf, one lung

cards.front: Why does the leaf's two-gap rule for water cost not apply to a human lung?
cards.back: Breathing moves air in bulk, and the airways wet incoming air and recover some water on the way out, so the cost must be worked out from one breath.
cards.quote: Breathing moves air in bulk, and the airways wet incoming air and recover some water on the way out
cards.section: Where the price comes from: one leaf, one lung

cards.front: Inhaled air is about 21% oxygen and exhaled air about 16%. Room air at 20 degrees C and half humidity holds about 1% water vapour; the nearly saturated breath out holds about 4 to 5% more. Estimate the water molecules lost per oxygen taken up.
cards.back: Oxygen taken up: 21 − 16 = 5% of the volume. Water added: about 4 to 5% of the volume. Ratio about 0.8 to 1, so roughly one water molecule per oxygen.
cards.quote: So the lung pays about one water molecule per oxygen
cards.section: Where the price comes from: one leaf, one lung

cards.front: A person breathes cold, dry air instead of room air. What happens to the water lost per oxygen taken up, and why?
cards.back: It rises. The lesson says cold, dry air raises the rough one-water-per-oxygen price of breathing.
cards.quote: a rough size that breathing rate, oxygen extraction and the air's temperature and humidity move (cold, dry air raises it)
cards.section: Where the price comes from: one leaf, one lung

cards.front: A barley leaf pays about 160 water molecules per carbon dioxide; a human lung pays about one water per oxygen. Using the rules for each, explain the difference.
cards.back: Leaf: the price is set by gaps, and carbon dioxide is scarce in air, so the CO2 gap is small while the water gap in dry air is about 100 times larger. Lung: breathing sets the price; about 5% of each breath is taken as oxygen, similar to the 4 to 5% water added.
cards.quote: with carbon dioxide scarce and the air inside the leaf close to saturated, the water gap is about a hundred times the carbon dioxide gap
cards.section: Where the price comes from: one leaf, one lung

cards.front: Water-use efficiency = {{c1::carbon gained / water lost}}, the price turned upside down.
cards.quote: water-use efficiency = carbon gained / water lost, the price turned upside down
cards.section: Worked problem: what a leaf pays

cards.front: Illustrative leaves under the same light and temperature: leaf A assimilates 20 umol CO2 and transpires 5 mmol H2O per m2 per s; leaf B, with fewer stomata, assimilates 16 and transpires 3. How far do B's carbon gain and water loss fall, and how does its water-use efficiency compare?
cards.back: Carbon: 16/20 = 0.8, 20% less. Water: 3/5 = 0.6, 40% less. Efficiency: A 20/5 = 4.0, B 16/3 = 5.33 umol CO2 per mmol H2O; B is 5.33/4.0 = 1.33 times A (about 190 vs 250 water molecules per CO2).
cards.quote: Its efficiency is 5.33 / 4.0 = 1.33 times A's.
cards.section: Worked problem: what a leaf pays

cards.front: When a leaf has fewer open stomata, why does its carbon gain fall less than its water loss?
cards.back: Carbon dioxide arrives more slowly while the cells keep fixing it, so CO2 inside the leaf falls and the CO2 gap widens, propping up carbon gain; water loss falls with conductance.
cards.quote: so its concentration inside the leaf falls and the carbon dioxide gap widens, propping up carbon gain while water loss falls with conductance
cards.section: Worked problem: what a leaf pays

cards.front: Depending on sun and wind, why might a leaf with fewer stomata save less water than the drop in conductance predicts?
cards.back: With less water evaporating, the leaf can run warmer, which widens the water vapour gap and gives back part of the saving.
cards.quote: with less water evaporating it can run warmer, depending on sun and wind, which would widen the water gap and give back part of the saving
cards.section: Worked problem: what a leaf pays

cards.front: Leaf A has more stomata than leaf B. Which does better when water is scarce, and which when water is plentiful and carbon limits growth?
cards.back: Water scarce: B, which keeps more water per unit of carbon gained. Water plentiful: A, which gains more carbon. Neither is better everywhere.
cards.quote: Neither leaf is better everywhere: when water is scarce, leaf B keeps more of it per unit of carbon gained
cards.section: Worked problem: what a leaf pays

cards.front: A leaf transpires 4 mmol H2O per m2 per s steadily for an 8-hour day. About how much water does it lose per m2, in kg? (Water is 18 g per mol.)
cards.quote: Over a 10-hour day (36,000 s), Leaf A loses 5 mmol x 36,000 = 180,000 mmol = 180 mol H2O per m2
cards.section: Worked problem: a 10-hour day

cards.front: Barley lines overexpressing HvEPF1 had far fewer stomata, and grain yield did not differ significantly from controls with five plants per group in a greenhouse. Why is "no yield loss detected" the right conclusion, rather than "fewer stomata cost no yield"?
cards.back: A non-significant difference in small groups is a non-detection, not proof of equal yield; a small loss could be missed. The tests were also in a greenhouse, not a field.
cards.quote: far fewer stomata, much less gas exchange, no grain loss detected
cards.section: A test in barley: what the film left out

cards.front: In barley engineered to make far fewer stomata, what happened in a separate test where water was withheld?
cards.back: The engineered lines kept photosystem II working about four days longer than controls.
cards.quote: the engineered lines kept photosystem II, part of the light-capturing machinery, working about four days longer than controls
cards.section: A test in barley: what the film left out

cards.front: In low-stomata HvEPF1 barley under water restriction, water-use efficiency from leaf carbon isotopes rose in both lines, but assimilation divided by stomatal conductance from gas exchange rose in neither. What does this show?
cards.back: Efficiency measures are not interchangeable: the isotope measure integrates over the flag leaf's life, the gas-exchange measure is a different ratio. A claim about efficiency must say which measure it uses.
cards.quote: rose in one line when well watered but in neither line under water restriction; the measures are not interchangeable
cards.section: The barley test: lines, watering levels and efficiency measures

cards.front: How do structures come to fit what they do, without anyone intending it?
cards.back: Individuals differ, some differences are inherited, and some inherited differences change how many offspring an individual leaves; over generations those variants become more common. That is natural selection.
cards.quote: Structures usually fit what they do because of history, not intention.
cards.section: Why structure fits function, and why never perfectly

cards.front: A heritable trait that natural selection shaped because it helped survival and reproduction is an {{c1::adaptation}}.
cards.quote: a heritable trait it shaped because it helped survival and reproduction is an adaptation
cards.section: Why structure fits function, and why never perfectly

cards.front: A trait that is useful now without having been selected for that use is sometimes called an {{c1::exaptation}}.
cards.quote: A trait can also be useful now without having been selected for that use; such a co-opted trait is sometimes called an exaptation.
cards.section: Why structure fits function, and why never perfectly

cards.front: Rewrite "barley has fewer stomata to save water" as an evolutionary claim with no goal in it.
cards.back: "In dry places, barley lineages with fewer stomata lost less water and left more descendants." The shorthand skips that history and reads as if the plant had a goal.
cards.quote: in dry places, barley lineages with fewer stomata lost less water and left more descendants
cards.section: Why structure fits function, and why never perfectly

cards.front: A single barley plant whose soil dries out makes fewer stomata on its new leaves. Is that plant evolving?
cards.back: No. A change within one plant's lifetime is a developmental response, a proximate matter; populations evolve across generations.
cards.quote: One plant changing its leaves within its own lifetime is a developmental response
cards.section: Why structure fits function, and why never perfectly

cards.front: Give three reasons the fit of structure to function is never perfect.
cards.back: Trade-offs between traits; history (selection starts from inherited structures); chance and by-products.
cards.quote: The fit is never perfect, for at least three reasons.
cards.section: Why structure fits function, and why never perfectly

cards.front: A {{c1::trade-off}} is a link between two traits such that improving one worsens the other.
cards.back: Example: more stomata raise capacity both to take in carbon and to lose water.
cards.quote: A trade-off is a link between two traits such that improving one worsens the other.
cards.section: Why structure fits function, and why never perfectly

cards.front: Structures inherited from a common ancestor and modified in each lineage, such as the human arm, bat wing and whale flipper, are {{c1::homologous}}.
cards.quote: They are homologous, inherited from a common ancestor and modified in each lineage
cards.section: Why structure fits function, and why never perfectly

cards.front: A whale flipper still contains an upper arm bone, two forearm bones, wrist bones and digits. Why, if selection shaped it for swimming?
cards.back: Selection reshaped bones the whale's ancestors already had; it began from them. Evolution does not move a population toward a preconceived ideal, so history constrains the fit.
cards.quote: Selection on a whale's ancestors could reshape those bones, but it began from them.
cards.section: Why structure fits function, and why never perfectly

cards.front: Give two ways a trait can spread or persist without being an adaptation.
cards.back: By chance, especially in small populations; or as a by-product of other features, not selected for itself (a spandrel).
cards.quote: Some traits spread by chance, especially in small populations, and some are by-products of other features, not selected for themselves.
cards.section: Why structure fits function, and why never perfectly

cards.front: Why is no living organism, such as a human compared with a honeybee, "more evolved" than another?
cards.back: Both lineages have had the same length of time since their common ancestor, and each has its own solutions to the same five problems.
cards.quote: a honeybee and a human have both had the same length of time since their common ancestor
cards.section: Why structure fits function, and why never perfectly

cards.front: Distinguish proximate from ultimate causes.
cards.back: Proximate causes act within an organism's lifetime (mechanism, development). Ultimate causes lie in the lineage's evolutionary history (adaptive significance, history); "ultimate" does not mean purpose.
cards.quote: proximate causes, which act within an organism's lifetime, from ultimate causes, which lie in the lineage's evolutionary history
cards.section: How questions and why questions

cards.front: Sort each question about barley stomata into Tinbergen's four: (a) how guard cells open and close the pore; (b) how genes such as HvEPF1 set stomata number; (c) whether density changes reproductive success in a field; (d) how density changed across grasses on a tree.
cards.back: (a) Mechanism, proximate. (b) Development, proximate. (c) Adaptive significance, ultimate. (d) History, ultimate.
cards.quote: In 1963 Niko Tinbergen set out four questions, and biologists now usually group them two to each kind
cards.section: How questions and why questions

cards.front: Which kinds of question does the HvEPF1 barley experiment answer, and which does it leave untested?
cards.back: Proximate questions in engineered lines: development (how HvEPF1 sets stomata number) and what fewer stomata do to gas exchange, water use and grain. It does not test how guard cells open and close, or any ultimate question.
cards.quote: The barley experiment answers proximate questions in engineered lines: the development row, and what fewer stomata do to gas exchange, water use and grain.
cards.section: How questions and why questions

cards.front: Guppy males introduced from a high-predation to a low-predation stream matured later than males of the source population. Design a test of whether the difference is inherited rather than a direct effect of food or water.
cards.back: Collect introduced and source fish at the same time and rear their descendants side by side in one laboratory environment (common garden), same food, temperature and density, for at least two generations.
cards.why: Two generations dilute effects passed on through the mother's condition.
cards.quote: rear their descendants side by side in one laboratory environment (a common-environment, or common-garden, design)
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In a common-garden assay of second-generation laboratory guppies, source-population males matured at 60.6 days and introduced-population males at 72.7 days. How much later did introduced males mature, in days and percent?
cards.quote: the adjusted mean male maturation ages were 60.6 days for source fish and 72.7 days for introduced fish
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A common-garden assay shows introduced guppies' later maturation is inherited. Why does that still not show predation caused it, and what comparison would?
cards.back: Moving fish above a waterfall may change density and food as well as predation. Compare several high- and low-predation streams and measure density and food at each.
cards.quote: Moving fish above a waterfall may change density and food as well as predation
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In a eusocial colony, how does a worker that does not reproduce still pass on copies of its genes?
cards.back: Indirectly, by helping raise close relatives.
cards.quote: A worker that does not reproduce still passes on copies of its genes indirectly, by helping raise close relatives.
cards.section: Reproduction without every individual reproducing

cards.front: Under what conditions do the leaf's two flow equations (carbon in, water out) hold?
cards.back: At steady state when the pores are the main resistance: a thin boundary layer, little water lost through the waxy layer, and air inside the leaf treated as saturated.
cards.quote: The two flow equations hold at steady state when the pores are the main resistance
cards.section: What the gap rule leaves out
